message.content:
The 19th‑century world’s most celebrated sculpture is almost universally regarded as **“The Thinker” (Le Penseur) by Auguste Rodin**. ### Why “The Thinker” stands out | Feature | Details | |---------|---------| | **Creation period** | 1880–1902 (first cast 1889) | | **Style** | Realist/Modernist – a departure from the idealized forms of neoclassicism | | **Iconic pose** | A seated male figure, head bowed, hand on chin – a universal symbol of contemplation | | **Cultural impact** | • Adopted as a motif in literature, philosophy, and popular culture.
• Replicated in bronze, marble, and other media worldwide.
• Frequently referenced in political and artistic discourse. | | **Legacy** | • Influenced generations of sculptors and modern art movements.
• Continues to be displayed in major museums (Musée Rodin, Paris; Musée d’Orsay, Paris; Musée des Beaux‑Arts, Lyon). | ### Other contenders While “The Thinker” is the most iconic, several other 19th‑century sculptures also achieved immense fame: | Sculpture | Artist | Year | Significance | |-----------|--------|------|--------------| | **The Kiss** | Auguste Rodin | 1889 | Celebrated for its sensual realism and emotional depth. | | **The Gates of Hell** | Auguste Rodin | 1880–1917 | A monumental frieze that redefined narrative sculpture. | | **The Statue of Liberty** | Frédéric Bartholdi | 1886 | Though a monument, it became a global symbol of freedom. | | **The Birth of Venus** (recast) | Alexandre Falguière | 1885 | A revival of classical myth with a modern twist. | ### Bottom line If you’re looking for the single sculpture that captured the imagination of the 19th‑century public and continues to be recognized today, **Rodin’s “The Thinker”** is the definitive answer. Its blend of technical mastery, philosophical resonance, and widespread reproduction cemented its place as the era’s most famous work of sculpture.
